302.title: Starting again
302.hook: refugee Sikh families rebuild from nothing in Delhi, East Punjab and beyond
302.howItsDone: Sikhs close the Ardas by asking for chardi kala, rising spirits, and many families from Partition speak of it together with kirat karni, honest work, when they tell how they rebuilt.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Partition: a land split in two. So what do you do the morning after you've lost everything?

A refugee train pulls into Delhi in the autumn of 1947, and a family climbs down with a bundle of clothes, a few pots and a brass water jug from home. Back home they had a farm, or a shop, or a house with a courtyard. Now they have a tent in a refugee camp and a number on a list. The father finds a cart and sells whatever he can buy cheap that morning. The mother takes in sewing. The children go to school under a tree. It will take years; some families will tell you it took a generation.
screen: `A BUNDLE, A FEW POTS.` → `A TENT AND A NUMBER.` → `A CART, A NEEDLE, A SCHOOL UNDER A TREE.`

segments.voice: In Delhi there was Kingsway Camp; near Kurukshetra, a huge camp of tents held a city's worth of people. Hindu and Sikh refugees from the west lived in them for months, some for years. Then the building began. Whole new neighborhoods went up in Delhi for refugee families, and you can still hear Punjabi from the older shops there. In East Punjab, families who had left farms were given land against what they'd lost, often less, and often worse, than what they left behind. They cleared it and planted anyway. Many moved on again, to other cities, and later across the world. Underneath all of this is a Sikh word you learned early on the path: chardi kala. Chardi means rising, climbing; kala is spirit, strength. Rising spirits, an unbeaten heart. It's said at the end of every Ardas, and it doesn't mean pretending things are fine. The families of 1947 grieved; many never spoke about what they saw. Chardi kala is grief and getting up at the same time. It sits beside another old teaching, kirat karni, earning an honest living with your own hands. A cart is honest work. So is a needle, or a small shop. Families still tell of a grandfather who started over late in life with nothing but that. Today's line has one extra word: again. Chardi kala isn't a mood you find once. It's something you choose again, the next morning, and the next.
screen: `THE CAMPS: KINGSWAY, KURUKSHETRA.` · `NEW HOMES, NEW FIELDS.` · `CHARDI KALA: RISING SPIRITS.` · `GRIEF AND GETTING UP, TOGETHER.` · then, large: `CHARDI KALA, AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Think of something you let go of when life got hard: a walk you used to take, a letter you meant to write, a few lines of reading. Don't scold yourself about why it stopped; just pick it up in your mind, the way you'd pick up a tool. Find the smallest possible first step, and let that decision settle with the breath.
Starting again. Refugee families of 1947 rebuilt from nothing, in tents, carts and new fields, with chardi kala: rising spirits, chosen again each day.
Your line: chardi kala, again. A cart, a needle, a small shop: that's how it began. See you tomorrow.

303.title: A Punjabi-speaking state, 1966
303.hook: after long campaigning, a smaller Punjab is formed around the Punjabi language
303.tomorrow: The daily prayer for open doors
303.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Punjabi Suba movement as a long, largely peaceful campaign; many gurdwaras still teach Gurmukhi so that Punjabi, the language of the Guru Granth Sahib's script, is kept.

segments.voice: Yesterday, starting again: chardi kala, again. Today the rebuilding turns to something you can't carry in a bundle: a language.

Some words don't survive translation. A grandmother's scolding in the language she grew up with. A family's private switch of tongue when the kids shouldn't follow. The name of a dish. The way people say goodbye at the door. A language carries all of that, which is why people will campaign for years to keep one. In the 1950s, India's map was being redrawn around languages, state by state. Punjabi speakers asked for a state of their own, and were told no.
screen: `WORDS THAT DON'T TRANSLATE.` → `THE MAP REDRAWN BY LANGUAGE.` → `PUNJABI SPEAKERS TOLD NO.`

segments.voice: After independence, Telugu speakers got a state of their own, and so did others. But when Sikh leaders asked for one built around Punjabi, the answer was no, for years. The campaign was called the Punjabi Suba movement, suba meaning a province. It was led by the Akali Dal, first under Master Tara Singh and later under Sant Fateh Singh. Its main tool was the morcha: a peaceful campaign in which volunteers marched, sang and courted arrest, wave after wave. Tens of thousands went to jail. Language had become tangled with religion and politics. Punjabi written in Gurmukhi, the script of the Guru Granth Sahib, was close to Sikh hearts. In the censuses of those years, many Punjabi-speaking Hindus, urged on by some Hindu organizations, recorded Hindi as their language instead. So the question was never only about grammar. Then, in 1966, after the war with Pakistan the year before, the government agreed. On the first of November 1966, Punjab was divided again, this time peacefully. The Hindi-speaking south became a new state, Haryana. Hill districts went to Himachal Pradesh. What remained was a smaller Punjab, with Punjabi in Gurmukhi as its language and Chandigarh held back as a shared capital. Not everyone was satisfied: arguments over Chandigarh and the river waters went on for decades, and they matter for the harder chapters ahead. But the language itself was kept: offices, street signs and school books in Punjabi, written in the script of the Guru Granth Sahib.

If you only have one language, find a word that belongs to your family alone, a nickname or a saying. Notice who it brings to mind, and let it keep you company for a few breaths.

304.title: The daily prayer for open doors
304.hook: for decades the Ardas asked for free access to the gurdwaras left behind
304.howItsDone: In the Ardas, said standing at the close of most Sikh gatherings, Sikhs ask for open access to, and the care of, Nankana Sahib and the other gurdwaras from which the Panth was separated in 1947.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Punjabi suba: the language kept. Today, back to 1947 one more time, for something Sikhs carried out of it into every single day.

A childhood house someone else lives in now. A grandparent's town across an ocean. A front door remembered exactly, that can't be walked through. For Sikhs after 1947, that door was Nankana Sahib, where Guru Nanak was born, and many other gurdwaras now across a border. The community didn't keep that longing for one anniversary a year. It put it into the prayer said every day.
screen: `A DOOR YOU CAN'T WALK THROUGH.` → `NANKANA SAHIB, ACROSS THE BORDER.` → `A LONGING PUT INTO A PRAYER.`

segments.voice: You've met the Ardas already: the standing prayer that closes nearly every Sikh gathering, said hands joined, facing the Guru Granth Sahib. It remembers the ten Gurus, then the Sikhs who gave their lives, and then it asks. It isn't a fixed text from one day in history; its core is old, and the community has added to it as the story went on. After Partition, a request was added. In plain English, it asks the Guru to grant the Khalsa free sight of, and the care and service of, Nankana Sahib and the other gurdwaras and holy places from which the Panth has been separated. The Punjabi phrase at its heart is khulle darshan didar: open sight, open visits. So ever since, in homes and gurdwaras around the world, Sikhs have asked every day for a door to open. A loss that could have turned bitter became a daily hope, said out loud, together. The door was not fully shut. Groups of pilgrims, called jathas, were allowed to cross for the big gurpurabs, under agreements between India and Pakistan. But for many Sikhs, a visit to Guru Nanak's birthplace stayed a lifelong hope. Many never went, and still the line was said. The request is in the Ardas today, because Sikhs still ask for open, free access to all the places they were separated from. It's a small lesson in holding a longing: not by forgetting it, not by letting it harden, but by praying it, gently, every day.

segments.voice: Let one long hope come to mind: a reconciliation, a healing, a place you want to see, a door you want opened, for you or for someone else. Don't push it or plan it; just let it be there. If you pray, offer it in your own words, the way the Sikh community has offered its hope for decades; if you don't, name it quietly to yourself and notice how long you've carried it.

305.title: Kartarpur corridor, 2019
305.hook: a corridor opens so pilgrims from India can visit Kartarpur, where Nanak farmed
305.howItsDone: Sikh pilgrims from India cross the Kartarpur corridor, when it is open, to visit Gurdwara Darbar Sahib, where Guru Nanak lived his last years; many Sikhs mark his birth anniversary there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ardas: since 1947, it has asked every day for open sight of the gurdwaras left behind. Open doors. Today, for one of those places, an answer came.

For years, at a town called Dera Baba Nanak, right on the Indian side of the border, there was a viewing platform. Pilgrims climbed up, some with binoculars, and looked across the fields. About four kilometers away, just visible on a clear day, stood a white gurdwara in Pakistan. People bowed to a building they could see but couldn't reach. Some came back year after year. Some grew old doing it. Then, in November 2019, a road opened.
screen: `A PLATFORM AT THE BORDER.` → `A WHITE GURDWARA, FOUR KILOMETERS AWAY.` → `NOVEMBER 2019: A ROAD OPENS.`

segments.voice: Kartarpur means the Creator's town. Guru Nanak founded it on the bank of the river Ravi after his long journeys, and spent the last years of his life there, about eighteen of them. What did he do there? He farmed. The Guru who had spent some twenty years on the road, across India and, tradition says, as far as Mecca and Baghdad, came home and worked the fields. Around him grew the first Sikh community: people who worked honestly, sang together morning and evening, and ate together. There Guru Nanak passed the light to Guru Angad, and there he died, in 1539. In 1947 the border put Kartarpur on the Pakistani side: close enough to see, too far to touch. Then, in 2019, the two governments opened a corridor: a road, a bridge and a crossing, so pilgrims from India could walk to the gurdwara without a visa and come back the same day. It opened on the ninth of November, days before the five hundred fiftieth anniversary of Guru Nanak's birth. People wept at the crossing. Old men who had stood on the platform for decades walked in. It hasn't been simple. The corridor has closed at times, during the pandemic and in periods of tension between the two countries. But for Sikhs it answered, in part, the prayer said every day since 1947. And it closes our long walk through Sikh history: from Banda Singh and the years in the forests, through the Misls and Maharaja Ranjit Singh, annexation and the gurdwara reform, to Partition and a door that opened.

306.title: Before we begin
306.hook: this week remembers a year of deep pain for Sikhs; we go slowly and blame no people as a whole
306.howItsDone: Sikhs remember 1984 each June and November with Ardas, kirtan and gatherings; many families also speak of it privately, and gently, at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kartarpur corridor: a road to the town where Guru Nanak farmed. The door opened, and our walk through Sikh history closed. This week is different, so today we pause at the door first.

Some dates, in some families, are said more quietly than others. Ask about 1984 in some Sikh homes, and there may be a long silence before an answer. Or a story about an uncle. Or a photograph brought out from a drawer. For many Sikh families, 1984 is a wound still within living memory. It isn't a chapter in a book; it's parents, neighbors, a childhood. So before this week begins, i want to stop for a day and talk about how to walk through it.
screen: `SOME DATES ARE SAID QUIETLY.` → `1984: A WOUND IN LIVING MEMORY.` → `FIRST, HOW TO WALK.`

segments.voice: Here's what this week holds. Tomorrow, Punjab in the early 1980s: how a political crisis became violent. Then June 1984, when the Indian army entered the Harmandir Sahib complex. Then a library that was lost. Then November 1984, when mobs killed thousands of Sikhs, mostly in Delhi. Then the long wait for justice, and finally how the Sikh community remembers. Now, how to walk. First: slowly. One piece a day, nothing told for drama. Second: carefully with the facts. Numbers, causes and people from these years are still argued about. Where accounts differ, i'll say so, and keep to what is widely documented. Third, and most important: no people as a whole are to blame. Governments and individuals made choices, and some committed terrible crimes. But no faith and no community is guilty as a whole. In November, there were Hindu neighbors who hid Sikh families in their homes at great risk. Sikhs themselves hold very different views about the people and choices of those years. This week asks you to hold more than one thing at once. Fourth: together. The Sikh word is sangat, the company of others on the path. Grief carried alone gets heavier; carried in company, it can be held. And fifth: you may stop. If this week is too heavy for you right now, you can wait. The path will still be here. That, too, honors the memory: coming to it when you can give it your full attention.

segments.voice: Take a few slow breaths and notice how you feel about going into this week: curious, heavy, unsure; whatever it is, it's allowed. Then make a quiet choice, to continue tomorrow or to wait a while and come back; either is fine, and nobody is keeping score. If you do continue, you might decide now who you'd talk to if something weighs on you.
Sangat. The company of others on the path — before this painful week begins, we go slowly, keep to what is documented, and blame no people as a whole.
Your line: gently, together. Nothing this week has to be carried alone. That's day three hundred six.

307.title: Punjab in the early 1980s
307.hook: political demands, rising violence and armed militants inside the Harmandir complex, led by Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale, a figure Sikhs see very differently, brought crisis
307.howItsDone: Sikhs hold a range of views on the early 1980s and on Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale; in gurdwaras and families these years are usually discussed with care, and often with strong feeling.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sangat: slowly, carefully with the facts, no people as a whole to blame. Gently, together. If you've chosen to continue, here is the first piece: how the crisis grew.

Some arguments start with something real: money, fairness, who gets a say. Nobody listens. Voices rise. A door slams. Then something happens that can't be taken back, and years later everyone involved tells the story differently, each holding a true piece of it. Punjab at the start of the 1980s was something like that, but with a whole state, a national government and many lives at stake.
screen: `AN ARGUMENT THAT STARTS WITH SOMETHING REAL.` → `NOBODY LISTENS.` → `EVERYONE HOLDS A TRUE PIECE.`

segments.voice: It began with politics. In 1973 the Akali Dal, the main Sikh party, passed the Anandpur Sahib Resolution, asking for more power for the states and for Chandigarh to be Punjab's. By the early 1980s, a fair share of Punjab's river waters was among the demands too. Governments in Delhi saw some of it as a threat to the nation. Talks went nowhere. In 1982 the Akalis began a new morcha, and tens of thousands of Sikhs courted arrest. Into this stepped Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale, the head of a traditional Sikh school, the Damdami Taksal. A powerful preacher, he called Sikhs back to amrit, to their practice, away from drink and drugs, and spoke fiercely about injustice to Sikhs. Meanwhile, violence grew in Punjab: killings of Hindus, of Sikhs who disagreed, of police, and hard police action in return. From 1982 Bhindranwale lived inside the Harmandir Sahib complex, and in December 1983 he and armed followers moved into the Akal Takht, which was fortified in the months that followed. Here is where to hold the whole story. Sikhs see Bhindranwale very differently. Some honor him as a saint and a martyr who stood up for a community they felt was treated unjustly. Other Sikhs believe his path, and weapons in the holiest place, led to disaster. The Indian government called him a terrorist. People in Punjab of every faith lived in fear in those years. This lesson doesn't settle who was right. It asks you to hold the demands, the grievances, the violence and the fear all at once, because they were all there.

308.title: June 1984
308.hook: the Indian army stormed the Harmandir complex during the martyrdom gurpurab of Guru Arjan; the Akal Takht was badly damaged and many pilgrims died
308.howItsDone: Each June, Sikhs gather at the Akal Takht and in gurdwaras worldwide for Ardas and kirtan in remembrance of those who died in 1984, and many light lamps or hold vigils.

segments.voice: Yesterday, morcha: demands, violence, fear, and a leader Sikhs see very differently. Hold the whole story. Today is the week's hardest day. Go gently.

Early June, in Amritsar, is hot. In 1984 it was also the time of a gurpurab: the day Sikhs mark the martyrdom of Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, who compiled the scripture and was put to death in Lahore. Families came to the Harmandir Sahib for it. Grandparents. Children. Villagers who'd saved for the trip. Many of them had nothing to do with politics. They came to bow, to hear kirtan by the water, to eat langar. And they were inside the complex when the army came.
screen: `EARLY JUNE: GURU ARJAN'S MARTYRDOM DAY.` → `FAMILIES COME TO THE HARMANDIR.` → `THEY WERE INSIDE.`

segments.voice: The government ordered the army to remove the armed militants from the complex. The operation was called Blue Star. A curfew was imposed across Punjab, and at the beginning of June the army surrounded the Harmandir Sahib. After days of firing, on the night of the fifth and sixth of June, troops entered, and tanks were used against the Akal Takht, where Bhindranwale and his fighters had fortified themselves. The Akal Takht, the seat of Sikh authority founded by Guru Hargobind, was badly damaged. Bhindranwale was killed. So were many soldiers, and many pilgrims caught inside. How many died is disputed. The government's own count was several hundred militants and civilians, and eighty-three soldiers. Many Sikhs, and many independent accounts, believe the true number was far higher, in the thousands, and that many of the dead were ordinary worshipers. Other gurdwaras across Punjab were entered at the same time. For Sikhs in Punjab and far beyond, it was a deep shock: the Harmandir Sahib attacked, on a holy day. Sikh remembrance at the Akal Takht calls it the third ghallughara, the third great massacre, after the two of the 1700s you learned about earlier. Afterward, the government repaired the Akal Takht. Sikhs refused that repair, took it down, and rebuilt it with their own hands, through kar seva, voluntary service. This week ran from starting again, a language kept, a prayer for open doors and a door opened, through a pause and a crisis, to this. Today, above all, remember the pilgrims.
screen: `OPERATION BLUE STAR.` · `THE AKAL TAKHT BADLY DAMAGED.` · `HOW MANY DIED IS DISPUTED.` · `THE THIRD GHALLUGHARA.` · then, large: `REMEMBER THE PILGRIMS.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle or a small lamp and it's safe, light it; if not, picture one, a small steady flame, standing for the pilgrims who came for a holy day and for everyone who died that June. You don't need names; just keep your eyes on the flame, or the picture of it, and breathe slowly. If you pray, remember them in your prayer; if you don't, let the flame do the remembering.
Ghallughara. A great massacre — what many Sikhs call June 1984, the third, when the army entered the Harmandir complex and the Akal Takht was badly damaged.
